blocks.text: Pandas gives you a huge library of built in operations: arithmetic, comparisons, string methods, group aggregations, all of it fast and all of it vectorized. But every now and then you need to do something to your data that none of those built ins were designed for. Maybe it is a business rule with three nested conditions, maybe it is a calculation that depends on values from five different columns at once, maybe it is a function someone on your team already wrote and you just need to run it on every row. That is exactly what .apply() is for. It is the escape hatch: the tool you reach for when nothing built in fits, letting you run any arbitrary Python function against a Series or a DataFrame.

This lesson covers how apply works on a Series versus a DataFrame, exactly what gets handed to your function in each case, when a lambda is enough and when you want a proper named function, and then the single most important thing to understand about apply: it is almost always slower than a vectorized operation, because underneath that clean looking syntax it is still just looping in Python. You will see that play out in a real before and after example, and then use apply the way it is actually meant to be used, as a genuine last resort.

blocks.alt: A funnel showing try a vectorized operation first, then np.where, then apply only as a last resort
blocks.caption: The order you should actually reach for these tools in.

blocks.text: 1. Series.apply: Running A Function On Every Value

The simplest form of apply lives on a Series. Call .apply(func) on a Series and pandas runs func once for every single value in that Series, then collects all the individual return values back into a brand new Series with the same index. It is conceptually identical to writing a Python for loop over the values and building up a list of results, just with pandas handling the bookkeeping for you.

blocks.alt: A Series of values flowing one at a time into a function, producing a matching new Series of results
blocks.caption: Series.apply calls your function once per value and stitches the results back together.

blocks.text: 1.1 A Basic Example

Say you have a Series of exam scores and you want to turn each numeric score into a letter grade. There is no built in pandas method for that specific mapping, so this is a genuinely custom per value rule, exactly the situation Series.apply exists for.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

scores = pd.Series([42, 88, 15, 67, 99])

def grade_label(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 50:
        return "C"
    return "F"

labels = scores.apply(grade_label)
print(labels)
# 0    F
# 1    B
# 2    F
# 3    C
# 4    A
# dtype: object

blocks.text: Pandas passed 42 into grade_label, got back "F", and stored that at index 0. It passed 88 in next, got back "B", stored it at index 1, and so on down the whole Series. Notice that grade_label itself is plain ordinary Python. It knows nothing about pandas or Series objects, it just receives one number and returns one string. That separation is exactly what makes apply so flexible: you write normal Python, and apply handles running it across every value.
1.2 When Series.apply Actually Earns Its Keep
Reach for Series.apply when the transformation you need genuinely cannot be expressed with a built in vectorized method, a string accessor, or a simple comparison. A handful of realistic situations:

items: Multi branch conditional logic that would need several chained comparisons to express as pure vectorized code.
Calling out to an external library function that only accepts one plain value at a time, with no array aware version available.
Parsing or reformatting messy text values with logic too specific for the built in str accessor methods.
Reusing an existing function someone already wrote elsewhere in the codebase, without rewriting it into array form.

blocks.title: Check the built ins first
blocks.content: Before writing an apply call, check whether pandas already has a method that does what you want. Series.str for text, Series.map for a simple dict style lookup, Series.where for conditional replacement. Apply should be what you fall back to, not the first tool you grab.

blocks.text: 2. DataFrame.apply: Rows Versus Columns

DataFrame.apply works the same basic way as Series.apply, run a function and collect the results, but a DataFrame is two dimensional, so pandas needs to know whether to feed your function one column at a time or one row at a time. That is controlled by the axis argument.

blocks.content: {"headers":["axis value","what gets passed to func","when you would use it"],"rows":[["axis=0, the default","one whole column, as a Series","a calculation that summarizes or transforms a single column at a time"],["axis=1","one whole row, as a Series","a calculation that needs values from several columns of the same row together"]]}

blocks.text: 2.1 axis=0: The Default, Column By Column
Leave axis unset, or set it explicitly to 0, and DataFrame.apply hands your function one entire column at a time, as a Series. Your function runs once per column, not once per cell.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame column flowing into a function as a whole Series, producing one result for that column
blocks.caption: With axis=0, the default, each call receives an entire column.

blocks.text: Here column_range ran twice total, once with the whole price column, once with the whole quantity column, not once per row. Each call got a full Series back with its own index, its own dtype, everything a normal Series has.
2.2 axis=1: Row By Row

Set axis=1 and the direction flips. Now DataFrame.apply hands your function one entire row at a time, again as a Series, where the index of that Series is the DataFrame's column names. This is the version you reach for whenever a calculation needs to combine values that live in different columns of the same row.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame row flowing into a function as a whole Series, producing one result for that row
blocks.caption: With axis=1, each call receives an entire row instead of a column.

code.content:
def row_total(row):
    return row["price"] * row["quantity"]

orders["total"] = orders.apply(row_total, axis=1)
print(orders)
#    price  quantity  is_vip  total
# 0    250         2    True    500
# 1     80         5   False    400
# 2    500         1    True    500
# 3    120         3   False    360

blocks.text: row_total ran four times, once per row of the DataFrame, and each time it received a Series holding that one row's price, quantity, and is_vip values, addressable by column name exactly like a dict.
2.3 Seeing Exactly What Gets Passed In
If the difference between axis=0 and axis=1 still feels abstract, the fastest way to make it concrete is to print what actually arrives inside the function.

code.content:
def inspect_row(row):
    print(type(row), row.name, row.index.tolist())
    return None

orders.apply(inspect_row, axis=1)
# <class 'pandas.core.series.Series'> 0 ['price', 'quantity', 'is_vip', 'total']
# <class 'pandas.core.series.Series'> 1 ['price', 'quantity', 'is_vip', 'total']
# ...

def inspect_col(col):
    print(type(col), col.name, col.index.tolist())
    return None

orders[["price", "quantity"]].apply(inspect_col, axis=0)
# <class 'pandas.core.series.Series'> price [0, 1, 2, 3]
# <class 'pandas.core.series.Series'> quantity [0, 1, 2, 3]

blocks.title: Row versus column, same object type
blocks.content: In both directions the function receives a genuine pandas Series, not a plain list or a dict. With axis=1, row.name is the row's index label and row.index is the list of column names. With axis=0, col.name is the column's name and col.index is the DataFrame's row index. Same object type, completely different contents.

blocks.text: 3. Lambda Versus A Named Function

Any function you pass to apply can be either a lambda written inline or a properly named function defined with def. Both work identically as far as apply is concerned. The choice is purely about readability and reuse.
3.1 Lambda For Quick Inline Logic

When the logic fits comfortably on one line and you are only going to use it in this one spot, a lambda keeps the code compact and keeps the transformation right next to the apply call where it is easy to read.

code.content:
orders["price_with_tax"] = orders["price"].apply(lambda p: p * 1.18)
print(orders["price_with_tax"])
# 0    295.0
# 1     94.4
# 2    590.0
# 3    141.6
# Name: price_with_tax, dtype: float64

blocks.text: 3.2 A Named Function For Anything Bigger

Once the logic grows past a single expression, needs a docstring, needs to branch on multiple conditions, or gets reused in more than one place in your codebase, switch to a proper named function. It is easier to test on its own, easier to give a descriptive name to, and easier for the next person reading the code to understand without mentally unpacking a dense one liner.

blocks.alt: Quick one line logic flowing to a lambda, complex or reused logic flowing to a named function
blocks.caption: Pick a lambda for one off one liners, a named function for anything bigger or reused.

items: Fits on one line and used once here: reach for a lambda.
Has branching logic, a docstring, or gets called from more than one place: write a named function.
Either way, apply itself does not care. It just calls whatever callable you give it.

blocks.text: 4. Why Apply Is Almost Always Slower

Here is the single most important practical lesson in this entire topic. Apply looks clean. It reads like a one line vectorized call, no visible for loop anywhere in your source code. But that appearance is misleading, and understanding why is what separates code that merely works from code that actually performs well on real sized data.
4.1 The Loop Hiding Under Clean Syntax

Underneath the hood, apply does not run your function inside NumPy's compiled C code the way a real vectorized operation does. It runs a plain Python loop, calling your function once per row, once per column, or once per value, exactly like writing that for loop yourself, just with pandas doing the looping instead of you typing it out. Every single call pays the full cost of the Python interpreter: looking up the function, pushing a new stack frame, running your Python bytecode, returning a value, and repeating that from scratch for every element.

blocks.alt: An apply call that looks vectorized on the surface but reveals a plain Python loop underneath, costing as much as a manual for loop
blocks.caption: Apply looks vectorized. Underneath, it is still a Python level loop.

blocks.text: On a hundred rows that overhead is invisible. On a million rows it becomes the entire bottleneck in your pipeline.
4.2 The Same Gotcha As np.vectorize

If you worked through the Vectorization lesson in the NumPy module, this should sound familiar. np.vectorize has the exact same trap: the name promises real vectorization, but it turns out to just be a Python level loop wearing a NumPy costume, calling your plain function once per element and stitching the individual results back together. pandas apply is built on that same underlying idea. The syntax is convenient. The looping is not gone, it has just moved somewhere you cannot see it directly in your own code.

blocks.title: Same lesson, different library
blocks.content: Anywhere you see a function that promises to run your custom Python logic across an array or a Series in one call, whether it is np.vectorize or DataFrame.apply, assume it is looping in Python underneath until proven otherwise. Convenient syntax is not the same thing as a performance win.

blocks.text: 4.3 Measuring It For Real
Numbers make this concrete. Compare applying a simple multiplication with apply against doing the exact same multiplication as a genuinely vectorized operation.

code.content:
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

n = 1_000_000
df = pd.DataFrame({"price": np.random.uniform(10, 500, n)})

start = time.time()
df["with_tax_apply"] = df["price"].apply(lambda p: p * 1.18)
apply_time = time.time() - start

start = time.time()
df["with_tax_vectorized"] = df["price"] * 1.18
vector_time = time.time() - start

print(f"apply time:       {apply_time:.4f} seconds")
print(f"vectorized time:  {vector_time:.4f} seconds")
print(f"speedup:          {apply_time / vector_time:.0f}x")
# apply time:       0.3841 seconds
# vectorized time:  0.0041 seconds
# speedup:          94x

blocks.text: Both lines compute the exact same result. The vectorized version runs the multiplication once, across the whole underlying NumPy array, inside compiled code. The apply version calls a Python lambda one million separate times. That gap only grows as your data grows.
5. Worked Example: Rewriting A Discount Calculation
Let's put the last section into practice with a realistic before and after. Start with the same small orders table from earlier: price, quantity, and whether the customer is a vip member.
5.1 The Naive Row Wise Apply Version

The rule: vip customers get 15 percent off, everyone else gets 10 percent off if they bought 3 or more items, and otherwise pays full price. It is tempting to reach straight for a row wise apply, since the rule reads naturally as an if else chain over a single row.

blocks.alt: A row with price and a vip flag flowing into an apply function that checks the flag and returns a discounted price
blocks.caption: The naive version: one Python function call per row, checking the flag each time.

blocks.text: This works correctly. It is also exactly the pattern from section 4: a Python function called once per row, with the interpreter overhead of a function call paid on every single one of those calls. On four rows nobody notices. On four million rows this becomes the slowest line in the whole script.
5.2 The Fully Vectorized Rewrite
Every piece of that logic is actually a simple comparison against a whole column, which means it can be expressed with boolean masking and np.where instead of a row wise loop.

blocks.alt: A boolean mask for vip rows feeding into np.where, which picks the correct discount and produces a discounted price column
blocks.caption: The vectorized rewrite: two boolean masks and one np.where call, no per row function calls at all.

code.content:
import numpy as np

vip_mask = orders["is_vip"]
bulk_mask = orders["quantity"] >= 3

orders["final_price"] = np.where(
    vip_mask,
    orders["price"] * 0.85,
    np.where(bulk_mask, orders["price"] * 0.90, orders["price"]),
)

blocks.text: vip_mask and bulk_mask are both computed with plain vectorized comparisons across the entire column at once. The outer np.where picks the vip discount wherever vip_mask is true, and falls through to the inner np.where for everyone else, which itself picks the bulk discount or the full price. No Python function gets called per row anywhere in this version, it is comparisons and array selection the whole way down.

blocks.content: {"headers":["approach","what actually runs","relative speed on large data"],"rows":[["Row wise apply","one Python function call per row, every single row","slow, scales linearly with row count and interpreter overhead"],["Boolean masking with np.where","a handful of whole column comparisons, compiled and vectorized","fast, the same handful of operations regardless of row count"]]}

blocks.text: 5.3 Apply As A Last Resort

This is the mindset to actually carry forward. Apply should be your last resort, reached for only when a genuinely custom per row or per element operation truly cannot be expressed as a vectorized operation at all. Before writing an apply call, spend a moment asking whether the same logic could be rewritten with boolean masking, np.where, np.select for more than two branches, or a built in vectorized method. Most row wise business rules that look like they need a Python if else chain can actually be rebuilt that way, exactly like the discount example above.

blocks.title: The apply performance gotcha
blocks.content: Apply will always produce a correct result. It will rarely produce a fast one on real sized data. Treat the clean looking syntax as a warning sign to double check for a vectorized alternative, not as proof that the code is already efficient.

blocks.text: 6. Returning Multiple Values: result_type Equals Expand

Sometimes the function you are applying naturally produces more than one output value per row, a total and a tax amount together, for instance. By default, if your function returns a tuple or a list, apply just stuffs that whole tuple into a single cell, giving you a Series where every entry is itself a small tuple. Passing result_type="expand" tells pandas to instead spread those returned values out across separate new columns.

blocks.alt: A row entering a function that returns three values, which result_type equals expand spreads out into three separate new DataFrame columns
blocks.caption: result_type equals expand turns one multi value return into several real columns.

blocks.text: 6.1 A Function That Returns More Than One Value
Extend row_total from earlier so it also works out the tax and the grand total, all three numbers computed together in one pass over the row.

code.content:
def price_stats(row):
    total = row["price"] * row["quantity"]
    tax = total * 0.18
    return total, tax, total + tax

result = orders.apply(price_stats, axis=1)
print(result)
# 0    (500.0, 90.0, 590.0)
# 1    (400.0, 72.0, 472.0)
# 2    (500.0, 90.0, 590.0)
# 3    (360.0, 64.8, 424.8)
# dtype: object

blocks.text: Without result_type set, each row's return value lands as one tuple crammed into a single cell of a Series with dtype object. That is rarely what you actually want to work with afterward.
6.2 Expanding Into New Columns
Add result_type="expand" and assign the result directly to a list of new column names, and each returned value lands in its own proper numeric column instead.

code.content:
orders[["total", "tax", "grand_total"]] = orders.apply(
    price_stats, axis=1, result_type="expand"
)
print(orders[["price", "quantity", "total", "tax", "grand_total"]])
#    price  quantity  total   tax  grand_total
# 0    250         2  500.0  90.0        590.0
# 1     80         5  400.0  72.0        472.0
# 2    500         1  500.0  90.0        590.0
# 3    120         3  360.0  64.8        424.8

blocks.title: Column count must line up
blocks.content: The number of column names you assign to has to match the number of values your function returns for every row. Return two values for one row and three for another and result_type="expand" will raise an error rather than silently padding the mismatch.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Classifying Orders Into Tiers

For a final worked example, apply a genuinely custom business rule: sort every order into a tier, and pick a shipping method to go with it, based on a combination of the order total and whether the customer is a vip. This is deliberately too specific and too branchy for a single simple vectorized comparison.

blocks.alt: An order row with amount, item count, and vip flag flowing into a custom business rule function that outputs a tier label of bronze, silver, or gold
blocks.caption: Classifying an order into a tier by combining several columns with a custom rule.

blocks.text: 7.1 A Rule That Needs Several Columns At Once
The business rule, straight from the product team:

items: If the order total is 1000 or more and the customer is vip, the order is platinum tier with priority shipping.
If the order total is 500 or more, on its own, the order is gold tier with standard shipping.
If the customer is vip but the total did not reach 500, the order is silver tier with standard shipping.
Everything else falls to bronze tier with standard shipping.

blocks.text: Notice this rule genuinely mixes two columns together and its branches are not a simple linear scale, platinum requires both a high total and vip status together, which is exactly the kind of tangled per row logic that justifies reaching for apply.
7.2 Implementing It With Apply

code.content:
def classify_tier(row):
    if row["total"] >= 1000 and row["is_vip"]:
        return "platinum", "priority shipping"
    elif row["total"] >= 500:
        return "gold", "standard shipping"
    elif row["is_vip"]:
        return "silver", "standard shipping"
    return "bronze", "standard shipping"

orders[["tier", "shipping"]] = orders.apply(
    classify_tier, axis=1, result_type="expand"
)
print(orders[["total", "is_vip", "tier", "shipping"]])
#    total  is_vip     tier             shipping
# 0  500.0    True     gold     standard shipping
# 1  400.0   False   bronze     standard shipping
# 2  500.0    True     gold     standard shipping
# 3  360.0   False   bronze     standard shipping

blocks.text: classify_tier receives a full row, checks total and is_vip together, and returns a pair of strings that result_type="expand" spreads into two clean new columns. None of the four sample rows here happen to hit the platinum branch, since none clears a total of 1000, but the branch is there and would fire the moment a big enough vip order came through.
7.3 Where A Simpler Version Would Have Been Vectorized

It is worth being honest about which part of this actually needed apply. If the rule had only been a single condition, say tier equals gold whenever total is 500 or more and bronze otherwise, that would have been a plain vectorized comparison, no apply required at all.

What pushed this particular example into apply territory was the combination: two columns considered together, three ordered branches, and two output values produced together per row rather than one. Even that is not entirely off the table for pandas. Tools like np.select can vectorize several ordered branches on a single column, and building two vectorized columns side by side could vectorize the tier and shipping outputs separately. But once real business rules start combining several columns with genuinely bespoke branching, apply frequently ends up being the clearest and most maintainable option, even knowing it costs you the vectorized speed. That tradeoff, clarity and correctness against raw performance, is one you get to make deliberately, as long as you understand what you are giving up.

blocks.caption: Ask whether it can be vectorized first. Apply is what is left when the answer is no.

blocks.text: 8.2 Key Takeaways

items: Series.apply runs your function once per value. DataFrame.apply runs it once per row with axis=1, or once per column with axis=0, the default.
A lambda is fine for a quick one line transformation used in one place. A named function is better once the logic grows or gets reused.
Apply looks vectorized but is not. It runs a Python level loop under the hood, exactly the same trap as np.vectorize from the NumPy module.
Before writing an apply call, check whether boolean masking, np.where, or np.select could express the same logic fully vectorized instead.
Use result_type="expand" whenever your function returns more than one value per row and you want each value in its own column.
Treat apply as a genuine last resort, reserved for logic that truly cannot be written as a vectorized operation, not as a default habit.
